before.excerpt:
Fix a category $\C$. The category laws, equality rules and arrow conventions
are those of Volume 0, Chapter~1. In this chapter, quantifiers over objects and typed
arrows have their stated categorical ranges; writing them does not assert
that those ranges form sets.

For example, to say that $(P,p,q)$ is a product of $A,B$ is to give the types
$p:P\to A$, $q:P\to B$ and require
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{for every object }X\text{ and all }
\alpha:X\to A,\ \beta:X\to B,\\
\text{there is exactly one }u:X\to P
\text{ with }p\circ u=\alpha,\quad q\circ u=\beta.
\end{gathered}
\]
This property does not assert that the displayed data exist. Having binary
products adds an outer existence claim for every pair of objects.

\begin{definition}[Four existence requirements]
\label{def:existence-requirements}
For a fixed category $\C$, consider the following assertions.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\Alph*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item[\textup{(T)}] There exists an object $T$ such that, for every object $X$,
there is exactly one arrow $X\to T$.
\item[\textup{(P)}] For every pair of objects $A,B$, there exist an object $P$
and arrows $p:P\to A$, $q:P\to B$ such that, for every object $X$ and all
$\alpha:X\to A$, $\beta:X\to B$, there is exactly one $u:X\to P$ with
$p\circ u=\alpha$ and $q\circ u=\beta$.
\item[\textup{(E)}] For every pair of objects $A,B$ and arrows $f,g:A\to B$,
there exist an object $E$ and an arrow $e:E\to A$ such that
$f\circ e=g\circ e$, and, for every object $X$ and every $h:X\to A$
satisfying $f\circ h=g\circ h$, there is exactly one $u:X\to E$
with $e\circ u=h$.
\item[\textup{(B)}] For every three objects $A,B,C$ and arrows
$f:A\to C$, $g:B\to C$, there exist an object $Q$ and arrows
$r:Q\to A$, $s:Q\to B$ such that $f\circ r=g\circ s$, and,
for every object $X$ and every pair $\alpha:X\to A$, $\beta:X\to B$
satisfying $f\circ\alpha=g\circ\beta$, there is exactly one $u:X\to Q$
with $r\circ u=\alpha$ and $s\circ u=\beta$.
\end{enumerate}
These say, respectively, that $\C$ has a terminal object, binary products,
equalizers of all parallel pairs, and pullbacks of all pairs with a common
target. They are assertions to be tested or assumed explicitly, not additional
axioms adopted by introducing this notation.
\end{definition}

Read (P) from outside inward: fix the two target objects, obtain one
product triple, and only then test it against arbitrary sources and
components.
The order of quantifiers matters. In (P), the product data may depend on
$A,B$, but must work for \emph{every} test $X,\alpha,\beta$. Choosing a
different candidate product for each test would not prove (P).
For (E) and (B), only compatible tests require factors. A construction
does not have to factor an ineligible test, and it does not supply test
arrows that have never been given.

after.excerpt:
Fix $\C$ as in Volume~0, Definition~\ref{def:category}.
For $A,B,P\in\operatorname{Ob}(\C)$ and $p:P\to A$, $q:P\to B$,
the product property is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
 &\forall X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\C)\quad
   \forall\alpha\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(X,A)\quad
   \forall\beta\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(X,B)\\
 &\qquad \exists!\,u\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(X,P)
   \quad(p\circ u=\alpha\ \land\ q\circ u=\beta).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
Condition (P) puts \(\forall A,B\;\exists(P,p,q)\) before this test.

\begin{definition}[Four existence requirements]
\label{def:existence-requirements}
Use the constructions from Volume~0, with $A,B,C\in\operatorname{Ob}(\C)$
in the formulas below.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
 (\mathrm T)\quad &\exists T\in\operatorname{Ob}(\C)\quad
   \forall X\in\operatorname{Ob}(\C)\quad
   \exists!\,u\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(X,T).\\
 (\mathrm P)\quad &\forall A,B\quad
   \exists(P,p,q)\ \text{a product of }A,B.\\
 (\mathrm E)\quad &\forall A,B\quad \forall f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(A,B)
   \quad \exists(E,e)\ \text{an equalizer of }f,g.\\
 (\mathrm B)\quad &\forall A,B,C\quad
   \forall f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(A,C)\quad
   \forall g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(B,C)\\
 &\qquad\exists(Q,r,s)\ \text{a pullback of }f,g.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\end{definition}

In (P), $(P,p,q)$ may depend on $A,B$. It is fixed before
$X,\alpha,\beta$ are chosen. In (E) and (B), the defining implication
restricts factorization to compatible tests (Volume~0,
Definitions~\ref{def:equalizer} and~\ref{def:pullback}).

before.excerpt:
\subsection*{Solution}
\paragraph{Exercise~\ref{ex:separate-inverse-equations}.}
\textup{(i)} Compare $g\circ(f\circ h)$ with $(g\circ f)\circ h$:
each hypothesis simplifies one adjacent pair.
The given arrows have types $f:A\to B$ and $g,h:B\to A$.
Thus $g\circ f:A\to A$ and $f\circ h:B\to B$.
Every row below compares arrows $B\to A$ and records its reason.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{$}l<{$} >{$}c<{$} l@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{1}{l}{Equality} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{Type} & Reason\\
\midrule
g=g\circ\id_B & B\to A & Right unit law.\\[3pt]
g\circ\id_B=g\circ(f\circ h) & B\to A & Substitute $f\circ h=\id_B$.\\[3pt]
g\circ(f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h & B\to A & Associativity.\\[3pt]
(g\circ f)\circ h=\id_A\circ h & B\to A & Substitute $g\circ f=\id_A$.\\[3pt]
\id_A\circ h=h & B\to A & Left unit law.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Reading the five equalities in order gives $g=h:B\to A$. The premise $g\circ f=\id_A$ gives one inverse equation for $g$.
Substituting $g=h$ into $f\circ h=\id_B$ gives the other:
\[
\begin{aligned}
g\circ f&=\id_A &&(A\to A),\\
f\circ g&=f\circ h=\id_B &&(B\to B).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are the equations in Definition~\ref{def:isomorphism}, so $f$ is an
isomorphism with inverse $g=h$.

\medskip
\noindent\textup{(ii)} Fix $f:A\to B$, and let $u,v:B\to A$ be any two
inverses of $f$. Take one inverse equation from each:
\[
u\circ f=\id_A\quad(A\to A),\qquad
f\circ v=\id_B\quad(B\to B).
\]
Apply part~\textup{(i)} with $g=u$ and $h=v$. Its types and hypotheses
match, so $u=v:B\to A$. Thus a fixed $f$ has at most one inverse.
This is an at-most-one statement; part~\textup{(i)} supplies existence
under its stated hypotheses.

after.excerpt:
\subsection*{Solution}
\paragraph{Exercise~\ref{ex:separate-inverse-equations}.}
\textup{(i)} From $f:A\to B$ and $g,h:B\to A$ we get
$g\circ f:A\to A$ and $f\circ h:B\to B$. Regrouping
$g\circ(f\circ h)$ lets us use both hypotheses.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{$}l<{$} l@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{1}{l}{Equality in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\C}(B,A)$} & Reason\\
\midrule
g=g\circ\id_B & Right unit law.\\[3pt]
g\circ\id_B=g\circ(f\circ h) & Substitute $f\circ h=\id_B$.\\[3pt]
g\circ(f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h & Associativity.\\[3pt]
(g\circ f)\circ h=\id_A\circ h & Substitute $g\circ f=\id_A$.\\[3pt]
\id_A\circ h=h & Left unit law.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The equalities give $g=h$. The given equation for $g$ and substitution
into the equation for $h$ give
\[
\begin{aligned}
g\circ f&=\id_A &&(A\to A),\\
f\circ g&=f\circ h=\id_B &&(B\to B).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are the equations in Definition~\ref{def:isomorphism}, so $f$ is an
isomorphism with inverse $g=h$.

\medskip
\noindent\textup{(ii)} Fix $f:A\to B$, and let $u,v:B\to A$ be any two
inverses of $f$. Take one inverse equation from each:
\[
u\circ f=\id_A\quad(A\to A),\qquad
f\circ v=\id_B\quad(B\to B).
\]
Apply part~\textup{(i)} with $g=u$ and $h=v$ to get $u=v:B\to A$.
This proves uniqueness whenever an inverse exists.

before.excerpt:
\begin{proposition}[Induction for an equation]
\label{prop:parameter-equality-induction}
Let $F,G:N\times B\to X$ under (A), and give their equalizer
$m:E\to N\times B$. Suppose their zero restrictions agree and
\[
F(s\times\id_B)m=G(s\times\id_B)m.
\]
Then $F=G$.
\end{proposition}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
The base equality makes $\langle z!_B,\id_B\rangle$ an eligible
equalizer test, giving a unique $b:B\to E$ with the required base
equation. The displayed step equality makes $(s\times\id_B)m$
another eligible test, giving $u:E\to E$ with
$m u=(s\times\id_B)m$. The parameter-induction proposition makes
$m$ invertible. Since $F m=G m$, precomposition with $m^{-1}$
in the equality gives $F=G$.
\end{proof}

An ``induction hypothesis''
for $F=G$ means using the equation on the equalizer source $E$;
the step must make the successor test factor back through that
same equalizer. If that is proved, the proposition establishes the
equation on all of $N\times B$.

Often both candidate maps already satisfy the same base and step
recursion. Then recursive uniqueness proves equality directly, with
no equalizer needed. We will use this shorter route whenever its
equations have been checked. Equality induction is useful when the
step calculation uses an equation known only on the represented part.

\begin{proposition}[Induction for an equation]
\label{prop:parameter-equality-induction}
Let $F,G:N\times B\to X$ under (A), and give their equalizer
$m:E\to N\times B$. Suppose
\begin{align*}
 F\langle z!_B,\id_B\rangle &= G\langle z!_B,\id_B\rangle,\\
 F(s\times\id_B)m &= G(s\times\id_B)m .
\end{align*}
Then $F=G$.
\end{proposition}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
The displayed equalities make $\langle z!_B,\id_B\rangle$ and
$(s\times\id_B)m$ eligible equalizer tests. Their unique factors
$b:B\to E$ and $u:E\to E$ satisfy
\[
 mb=\langle z!_B,\id_B\rangle,\qquad mu=(s\times\id_B)m.
\]
Parameter induction makes $m$ invertible, so
$F=Fm m^{-1}=Gm m^{-1}=G$.
\end{proof}

An ``induction hypothesis''
for $F=G$ means using the equation on the equalizer source $E$;
the step must make the successor test factor back through that
same equalizer. If that is proved, the proposition establishes the
equation on all of $N\times B$.

Often both candidate maps already satisfy the same base and step
recursion. Then recursive uniqueness proves equality directly, with
no equalizer needed. We will use this shorter route whenever its
equations have been checked. Equality induction is useful when the
step calculation uses an equation known only on the represented part.

before.excerpt:
\begin{problem}[A map is determined on the natural embedding]
\label{ex:integer-map-determined}
Let $u,v:Z\to H$ be group homomorphisms with $u j=v j$.
Prove $u=v$ without selecting a pair representative for
every arrow into $Z$.
\end{problem}

\paragraph{Solution.}
For the single supplied regular cover $q:P\to Z$,
$u q(a,b)=u j a-u j b=v j a-v j b=v q(a,b)$.
These are equations of maps $P\to H$. Epicity of $q$
then gives $u=v$. The argument never constructs a section
of $q$ or a representation for an arbitrary parameter arrow.
